text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers on Thursday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish commercial bank Handelsbanken's prospectus for its proposed buy of mortgage bank Stadshypotek AB was small and may be insufficient to convince investors about the deal, according to the paper's stock market commentator.
When Skandia bid for Stadshypotek, the insurance company had a significantly fuller prospectus in order to convince the shareholders about the deal's advantages.

- International financier George Soros, which in Wednesday's edition of the paper said a free market is a danger to democracy, has reaped his largest profits on regulated markets, the paper's stock market commentator said.
- Norwegian travel agents have turned to domestic competition authorities for support in their fight with Scandinavian Airlines (SAS) about provisions on tickets sold.

The travel agents say that SAS is abusing its strong position when proposing a bonus system for travel agents to compensate for plans to cut agents' provisions on domestic and intra-Scandinavian flights as of April 1.
- Sweden's competition authority is threatening Norwegian-owned Nitro Nobel with fines for using its dominating position on the explosives market.
- Recent above-zero temperatures in Sweden mean electricity prices on the Norwegian-Swedish electricity bourse are nearing collapse. Prices have fallen 22 percent in busy trade in only one week.
- Telecommunications group Ericsson leads companies on the Stockholm bourse which have a market capitalisation of more than one billion crowns, recently bypassing drug company Astra.
- No serious bidders have emerged for the state's 34 percent stake of Stadshypotek since Handelsbanken's bid was announced on December 12, finance ministry sources say.

- Handelsbanken did poorly in 1994, which was marked by rising debt yields, when its U.S. bonds alone fell in value by over 670 million crowns. Now Swedish tax authorities are threatening the bank with taxes totalling 301 million crowns.
- Violence among immigrant women and threats from their husbands stems from powerlessness felt by the husbands in their new countries, researchers say.

- Tax officials, acting upon policy directives to bring in revenues equal to 10 times their annual salaries, have collected 2.1 billion crowns in extra taxes from companies for 1995, a project in which the government invested 200 million crowns. But the project has now been called into question by the Department of Taxation, which opposes the requirement of a certain yield.

- The minority Social Democratic government and representatives of opposition policital parties held talks about the implementation of pension reform adopted by a previous government. At stake is about 60 billion crowns in a special reserve. In the year 2000, Swedish workers are supposed to be given a choice over whether to have these pension savings managed by private or public funds. But if the funds would be removed from the public economy, public finances would worsen, Prime Minister Goran Persson says.

- Scandinavian airline SAS said it filed a complaint with the European Union Commission over Alitalia's restructuring plan. In November, Alitalia unveiled a restructuring plan that calls for $965 million in fresh capital from its government.
